overview: I6102 combines the arrival methods that can put a student behind the aircraft quickly: arcing to final, radar vectors to final, localizer precision and non-precision work, and holding descents. The event standard is to compute lead points early, set D LIDS before intercept, transition to BAC on time, and keep holding corrections alive while changing altitude.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Arcing is used to position the aircraft inbound on an intermediate or final approach course by flying a constant DME from the NAVAID.

children.text: Expect arcing approaches to be identified by VOR/DME or TACAN in the approach margin; DME is required.
About 5 NM prior to the IAF, slow to 150 KIAS and have the arc direction, lead point, segment altitude, inbound course, and voice-report requirement ready.
At the IAF, use the 6 Ts, turn to place the bearing-pointer head on the 90-degree benchmark, comply with segment altitudes, and set the inbound course in the CDI.
Published lead radials marked LR-xxx are advisory and based on 200 KTAS with a half-standard-rate turn; at normal 150 KIAS approach speeds, compute the lead radial for a standard-rate turn.
For a radial-to-arc intercept, lead the arc by turn radius: 0.5 percent of groundspeed for standard-rate, or 1.0 percent of groundspeed for half-standard-rate.
For an arc-to-radial intercept, compute radials per NM as 60 divided by arc DME, then multiply by turn radius to find the no-wind lead radial.
If groundspeed is unavailable in time, KIAS may be used as a no-wind approximation, then adjusted for known wind.
On the arc, bearing-pointer head on the 90-degree benchmark holds DME in no wind; below the benchmark increases DME, and above it decreases DME.
If inside the arc, maintain heading or place the bearing-pointer head up to 15 degrees below the benchmark; if outside, place it up to 15 degrees above.
Within 5 NM of the FAF, transition to BAC as required and continue the published low-altitude approach procedure.

items.text: RVFAC uses ATC radar vectors to place the aircraft on the final approach course by the most expeditious route consistent with traffic and terrain clearance.

children.text: Fly 200 KIAS on downwind, 150 KIAS on base, and 200 KIAS on an extended final or extended dog-leg until within 15 NM of the airport.
Tune and identify the NAVAID, verify the PFD source, set the final approach course in the CDI, and follow assigned headings and altitudes.
ATC uses MVA for terrain clearance while vectoring, but maintain your own situational awareness with available NAVAIDs and charts; query if the vector or altitude does not make sense.
Transition to BAC when within 5 NM of the FAF and the aircraft heading is within 90 degrees of the final approach course.
If no FAF is depicted, transition to BAC once established on the final approach course and cleared for the approach.
After approach clearance, maintain the last assigned heading and altitude until established on the approach, then lead the turn as the CDI centers.

items.text: ILS is the precision approach in this event: localizer provides azimuth, glideslope provides vertical guidance, and DA/DH replaces the non-precision MDA decision model.

children.text: The T-6B is a Category I aircraft, and its single-piloted classification restricts planning to no lower than a 200-foot ceiling and 1/2 SM visibility.
If the localizer is inoperative, the ILS is not authorized; if the glideslope is inoperative, fly the LOC non-precision procedure and minimums.
Set the front course in the CDI, confirm the correct localizer identifier, and remember the localizer is four times more sensitive than VOR guidance.
Use D LIDS before intercept: DME hold if required, localizer tuned and identified, inbound course set, display source to LOC, and speed appropriate to the transition.
Transition to BAC in accordance with the transition procedure, or use glideslope alive at the published intercept altitude as an alternate cue.
At glideslope intercept, set about 24 percent torque, descend on course and glideslope at 120 KIAS, and adjust power for glideslope while using pitch primarily for airspeed.
Start backup timing at the non-precision FAF if timing is available, even when the ILS is working.
If full-scale CDI deflection occurs before the FAF, reintercept and do not descend below the glideslope-intercept altitude until on scale.
If more than one dot below glideslope, descend no lower than LOC MDA until reestablished or until the non-precision MAP.
If more than two dots above glideslope, continue as a LOC-only non-precision approach rather than forcing an unstable recapture.
At DA/DH, continue only with the runway environment in sight and a safe landing assured; otherwise execute the missed approach.

items.text: A localizer approach uses the localizer component of the ILS for lateral guidance, but it is a non-precision approach flown to MDA and MAP.

children.text: The localizer intercept and D LIDS setup are the same discipline as ILS: DME hold if required, tune and identify localizer, set inbound course, select LOC, and use transition speed.
On an ILS or LOC approach where the glideslope is unavailable or not used, fly non-precision rules and minimums.
If CDI is full-scale before the FAF, reintercept; if not on scale by the FAF, do not descend below FAF altitude.
At the non-precision FAF, perform the 6 Ts and start timing as MAP backup if timing is available.
Set about 20 percent torque, trim for a 120 KIAS descent, and keep descent rate stabilized at no more than 1000 fpm.
About 100 feet prior to MDA, set roughly 42 percent torque and transition to level flight at or above MDA.
If full-scale CDI deflection occurs between FAF and MAP, turn to reestablish and track while climbing to missed-approach altitude, then fly the missed at the MAP or as assigned.
Do not execute the missed just because MDA is reached; continue to the MAP unless safety, ATC, or loss of usable guidance requires otherwise.
Common errors are late D LIDS, flying through final, no backup timing, overcontrolling localizer corrections, using the wrong MDA, and continuing with full-scale CDI inside the FAF.

items.text: Holding keeps the aircraft inside protected airspace until ATC issues further clearance; the task is geometry, timing, correction, and communication all at once.

children.text: Start slowing within 3 minutes or 5 NM of the holding fix when clearance beyond the fix has not been received; normal T-6B holding airspeed is 150 KIAS.
A full uncharted holding clearance includes direction from fix, fix name, radial/course/bearing/route, leg length, turn direction, EFC, and delay information.
If the pattern is charted, hold as published unless ATC issues different instructions; if instructions are missing before an en route clearance limit, request them.
A standard pattern uses right turns; non-standard uses left turns. Inbound legs track the holding course, and outbound legs fly headings.
For standard entries, use parallel when the reciprocal lies between the heading index and 110 degrees left, teardrop when between the heading index and 70 degrees right, and direct otherwise.
For non-standard entries, reverse the entry-side logic. If the reciprocal is within 5 degrees of a boundary, either adjacent entry is acceptable.
At the end of the outbound leg, use tail-radial-turn to decide the inbound turn and establish on course promptly.
Use the no-wind orbit to measure wind: start timing when wings level or abeam, turn inbound toward the holding radial, then note crab angle and inbound time.
On correction orbits, triple the inbound drift correction outbound for no more than one minute, then use single drift if the outbound leg continues.
Adjust outbound timing by the inbound timing error; if inbound was 10 seconds short, add 10 seconds outbound.
Report established in holding with position, time, and altitude when required, and confirm EFC at least 5 minutes prior if it has not been confirmed.

items.text: A shuttle descent is an ATC-directed descent within holding that moves the aircraft to the next lower stack altitude while preserving protected-airspace control.

children.text: Shuttles are normally used after the lower aircraft in the stack has commenced the approach; vertical separation in the stack can be as little as 1000 feet.
Report leaving the current altitude for the assigned altitude, reduce power to about 15 percent torque, lower the nose to maintain 150 KIAS, and re-trim.
Lead the level-off about 50 feet prior, reset power near 33 percent torque, raise the nose to level flight, and re-trim.
Keep the holding correction alive during the descent; the altitude change does not pause timing, drift correction, or protected-airspace responsibility.
Common errors are fixating on altitude and losing the pattern, fixating on the pattern and missing level-off, or letting airspeed drift away from 150 KIAS.

studyNotes.summary: Compute arcing leads before the fix, set localizer approaches early with D LIDS, obey ILS/LOC deviation gates, and keep holding/shuttle descent corrections organized.

summary: Arcing approaches, RVFAC ILS/LOC work, holding, and shuttle descents.
title: Arcing and Holding
